content.question: A sensor reports temperature every second. Find the hottest 5-second window in a million readings. Brute force sums every possible window of 5 — that's ~5 million additions. But what if each new window only differs from the previous by ONE element entering and ONE leaving?

content.prompt: Find the maximum sum of any subarray of size k. Complete the sliding window logic.
content.hint: The element leaving is at index i - k. The element entering is at index i.

content.text: Imagine reading a book through a magnifying glass that shows exactly 3 lines at a time. To read line 4, you don't re-read lines 2 and 3 — you just shift the glass down one line. The OLD line 1 disappears from view, the NEW line 4 appears. That "shift" is the sliding window. Fixed window = magnifying glass always shows exactly k items. Variable window = a rubber band that stretches and shrinks based on a condition (like "keep expanding until the sum exceeds a limit, then shrink from the left").

content.annotation: Fixed window uses windowSum += arr[i] - arr[i - k] — one add, one subtract per slide. Variable window uses left and right pointers where right always advances and left catches up when a condition is violated. For "longest substring without repeats," when lastSeen.containsKey(c) finds a duplicate, we jump left past the previous occurrence. Time O(n) because each element is added and removed at most once.

content.modification: What if we remove the `&& lastSeen.get(c) >= left` check?
content.question: What does longestUniqueSubstring("abba") return without that condition?
content.explanation: Without the >= left check, when right reaches the second 'a' at index 3, lastSeen.get('a') returns 0, so left is set to 1. But left was already at 2 (moved there when the second 'b' triggered lastSeen.get('b') = 1, setting left = 2). Moving left BACKWARD from 2 to 1 breaks the window — it now includes the duplicate 'b'. The condition lastSeen.get(c) >= left ensures we only advance left forward, never backward.

content.question: Why is sliding window O(n) while brute force is O(n*k)?
options: Each element is added and subtracted exactly once via windowSum += arr[i] - arr[i - k]
content.explanation: Brute force recomputes windowSum from scratch for each position — k additions per window via the inner for-loop over j. Sliding window reuses the previous windowSum by executing windowSum += arr[i] - arr[i - k] — one addition and one subtraction per slide regardless of k. Total work is n elements × 2 operations = O(n).
